title: Historical Phonology
full_title: Chinese Historical Phonology: The Sounds of Earlier Chinese
tagline: Why historical phonology matters, fanqie spellings, the *Qieyun* and *Guangyun*, the initials of Middle Chinese, its finals and tones, rhyme tables, Old Chinese, from Middle Chinese to Mandarin, and phonology for readers
summary: Chinese characters do not show how they sounded, yet poets rhymed and scholars recorded sounds for two thousand years. This course explains how the sounds of earlier Chinese are reconstructed: fanqie spellings, the rhyme dictionaries from the *Qieyun* to the *Guangyun*, the categories of Middle Chinese, the rhyme tables, the evidence for Old Chinese, and the changes that led to modern Mandarin — and shows how this knowledge helps in reading classical poetry and understanding the dialects.

chapters.title: Why historical phonology?
chapters.summary: Old poems that no longer rhyme, the reputation of phonology as a forbidding subject, and what it is good for.

chapters.title: Fanqie spellings
chapters.summary: Spelling the sound of a character with two others, how fanqie works, and how it is used to recover old pronunciations.

chapters.title: The rhyme dictionaries
chapters.summary: Lu Fayan’s *Qieyun* of 601, the *Guangyun* of 1008, and its 206 rhymes.

chapters.title: The initials of Middle Chinese
chapters.summary: The thirty-six initials, and how the initial categories are worked out from fanqie.

chapters.title: The finals and tones of Middle Chinese
chapters.summary: Rhyme groups, divisions, open and closed finals, and the four tones: level, rising, departing and entering.

chapters.title: Rhyme tables
chapters.summary: The *Yunjing* and the *Qieyun Zhizhang Tu*, and how the tables lay out the sound system.

chapters.title: Old Chinese
chapters.summary: The evidence of the rhymes of the *Book of Songs* and of phonetic series, the rhyme groups of the Qing scholars, and modern reconstructions.

chapters.title: From Middle Chinese to Mandarin
chapters.summary: The *Zhongyuan Yinyun* of 1324, the loss of the entering tone, the splitting of tones by voicing, and palatalisation.

chapters.title: Phonology for readers
chapters.summary: Reading the rhymes and tones of classical poetry, explaining correspondences between dialects, and solving puzzles in old texts.
